title: Sending Flowers Is Easy. Showing Up Is Hard.
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership post argues that the difference between good and great leaders is not the gesture of sending flowers or a note but the willingness to physically show up. The author contrasts the expected big-moment appearances (milestones, award ceremonies) with the quieter, smaller occasions, such as a modest retirement party, a brief hospital visit, or a funeral for someone the leader barely knew. The central move is to reframe presence as the real currency of compassion: it costs the leader time and comfort, and that cost is exactly what signals care. The piece closes by claiming that people remember who was there long after they forget what was said or given, and that loyalty is built from these small moments. It ends with a memorable line, that great leaders do not send flowers, they bring them.
points: Showing up in small, low-profile moments of significance builds more loyalty than polished gestures at big public events.
The discomfort and inconvenience of attending are what make a leader's presence symbolic of genuine care.
Leaders earn the right to show up by learning what matters to their people: their milestones, challenges and relationships.
People remember who was present when it mattered, not the words or gifts, so presence is the durable form of recognition.
quotes: They attend the retirement party that feels painfully small. They make the hospital visit that could seem too brief to matter. They don’t just send flowers when a team member loses a loved one. They show up at the service even though they barely know anyone.

They recognize that what represents an inconvenience of time and travel to them can mean everything to someone else. They make it their business to know what matters most to people—the milestones they are working toward, the challenges they are facing, and the relationships they cherish.

Showing up in moments significant to others is often uncomfortable and awkward. The best leaders push through their discomfort and show up anyway because they know their presence is symbolic for how much they care.
Years and decades later, people still remember who was there. They don’t recall what was said, what was given, or what the weather was like. But they know who showed up when it mattered most.
We can sum up how the best leaders think about displaying their compassion for others: They don’t send flowers. They bring them.
